name: Coagulation cascade
summary: Secondary hemostasis: a cascade of zymogens, each activated by the one before, ending in thrombin and a cross-linked fibrin clot. Intrinsic: XII (contact) → XIIa activates XI → XIa activates IX → IXa with VIIIa (intrinsic tenase) activates X; measured by the PTT. Extrinsic: tissue factor with VIIa activates X; measured by the PT/INR. Common: Xa with Va (prothrombinase) turns prothrombin into thrombin, which turns fibrinogen into fibrin, activates V, VIII and XIII (XIIIa cross-links fibrin) and, on thrombomodulin, activates protein C. Off switches: antithrombin (thrombin, Xa; heparin), activated protein C with protein S (Va, VIIIa). Fibrinolysis: tPA turns plasminogen into plasmin, which breaks fibrin into degradation products (D-dimer). Vitamin K–dependent: II, VII, IX, X, proteins C and S (warfarin). Ca²⁺ and phospholipid for the tenases and prothrombinase.
tissue: blood plasma, on activated platelets (factors made in the liver; VIII also by endothelium)

f12.name: Factor XII
f12.notes: Hageman factor. Deficiency prolongs the PTT but causes no bleeding (it may even predispose to clots).

f11.name: Factor XI
f11.notes: Deficiency is hemophilia C (Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry): mild bleeding, prolonged PTT.

f9.name: Factor IX
f9.notes: Deficiency is hemophilia B (X-linked recessive): hemarthroses, prolonged PTT, normal PT. Vitamin K–dependent: made in the liver and γ-carboxylated by γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which needs reduced vitamin K. Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), so it falls on warfarin.

f7.name: Factor VII
f7.notes: Shortest half-life of the vitamin K–dependent factors, so the PT rises first when warfarin starts or the liver fails. Vitamin K–dependent: made in the liver and γ-carboxylated by γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which needs reduced vitamin K. Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), so it falls on warfarin.

f7a.name: Factor VIIa
f7a.notes: With tissue factor it starts coagulation in vivo (the extrinsic pathway, measured by the PT). Recombinant VIIa treats bleeding in hemophilia with inhibitors.

f8.name: Factor VIII
f8.notes: Carried in plasma by von Willebrand factor, which protects it; vWF disease can lower VIII. Deficiency is hemophilia A (X-linked recessive), the most common hemophilia; treat with factor VIII concentrate, desmopressin in mild cases.

f8a.name: Factor VIIIa
f8a.notes: Cofactor of IXa in the intrinsic tenase. Inactivated by activated protein C (with protein S).

f10.name: Factor X
f10.notes: Where the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways meet: the start of the common pathway. Vitamin K–dependent: made in the liver and γ-carboxylated by γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which needs reduced vitamin K. Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), so it falls on warfarin.

f10a.name: Factor Xa
f10a.notes: Inhibited by antithrombin (much faster with heparin; LMWH and fondaparinux mostly act here) and directly by rivaroxaban, apixaban and edoxaban.

f5.name: Factor V
f5.notes: Factor V Leiden (Arg506Gln) resists cleavage by activated protein C: the most common inherited thrombophilia.

f5a.name: Factor Va
f5a.notes: Cofactor of Xa in the prothrombinase. Inactivated by activated protein C (with protein S).

f2.name: Prothrombin
f2.notes: Prothrombin G20210A (3′ untranslated region) raises prothrombin levels: an inherited thrombophilia. Vitamin K–dependent: made in the liver and γ-carboxylated by γ-glutamyl carboxylase, which needs reduced vitamin K. Warfarin blocks vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), so it falls on warfarin.

f2a.name: Thrombin
f2a.notes: The cascade’s amplifier: cuts fibrinogen and activates V, VIII, XI and XIII, and activates platelets (PAR-1). Inhibited by antithrombin (with heparin) and directly by dabigatran, argatroban and bivalirudin. With thrombomodulin it turns on protein C instead.

fbg.name: Fibrinogen
fbg.notes: Also bridges platelets through GPIIb/IIIa. An acute-phase reactant; low in DIC.

f13.name: Factor XIII
f13.notes: Deficiency: delayed bleeding (e.g. from the umbilical stump) with normal PT and PTT.

xfbn.name: Cross-linked fibrin
xfbn.notes: Plasmin (from plasminogen, via tPA) breaks it down, releasing D-dimers.

pc.name: Protein C
pc.notes: Vitamin K–dependent anticoagulant made in the liver. Short half-life like VII, so warfarin lowers it first: transient hypercoagulability (warfarin skin necrosis, worst in protein C deficiency); bridge with heparin.

apc.name: Activated protein C
apc.notes: With its cofactor protein S, cuts and inactivates Va and VIIIa. Factor V Leiden resists it (activated protein C resistance). Protein S deficiency does the same.

at.name: Antithrombin
at.notes: Inhibits thrombin and Xa (also IXa, XIa, XIIa). Heparin makes it about a thousand times faster: unfractionated heparin acts on thrombin and Xa, LMWH and fondaparinux mostly on Xa. Deficiency (inherited, or lost in nephrotic syndrome): venous clots and little response to heparin.

plg.name: Plasminogen
plg.notes: Binds fibrin, so it is activated right where the clot is.

plasmin.name: Plasmin
plasmin.notes: Breaks down fibrin and fibrinogen (and cleaves factors V and VIII, activates complement). Aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid block its activation; α2-antiplasmin inhibits it.

fdp.name: Fibrin degradation products
fdp.notes: D-dimer comes only from cross-linked fibrin: high in DVT/PE and DIC; a normal D-dimer helps rule out a clot when pretest probability is low.

f10ext.name: Factor X
f10ext.notes: The same factor X, drawn twice: here the extrinsic tenase (tissue factor–VIIa) activates it.

contact.name: Contact activation
contact.notes: Factor XII is activated on negatively charged surfaces (collagen, glass, kaolin in the PTT test) with prekallikrein and high-molecular-weight kininogen. Kallikrein also makes bradykinin; C1 inhibitor blocks kallikrein (its deficiency causes hereditary angioedema).

tf.name: Tissue factor
tf.notes: Exposed when the vessel wall is injured; binds factor VII and lets it activate. The PT test adds tissue factor to plasma.

itenase.name: Intrinsic tenase (IXa + VIIIa)
itenase.notes: IXa with its cofactor VIIIa on the platelet phospholipid surface, with Ca²⁺. Makes most of the Xa once clotting is under way.

etenase.name: Extrinsic tenase (tissue factor–VIIa)
etenase.notes: Starts clotting: the first bit of Xa (and IXa). Quickly shut down by tissue factor pathway inhibitor (TFPI).

pthase.name: Prothrombinase (Xa + Va)
pthase.notes: Xa with its cofactor Va on the platelet phospholipid surface, with Ca²⁺.

thrombin.name: Thrombin
thrombin.notes: Its feedback (activating V, VIII and XI) turns a trickle of thrombin into a burst.

e13a.name: Factor XIIIa
e13a.notes: A transglutaminase: cross-links fibrin (glutamine to lysine), which needs Ca²⁺.

tm.name: Thrombin–thrombomodulin
tm.notes: Thrombin bound to thrombomodulin on intact endothelium stops cutting fibrinogen and activates protein C instead: clotting switches itself off away from the injury.

tpa.name: Tissue plasminogen activator
tpa.notes: Released by endothelium; works best on plasminogen bound to fibrin. Recombinant tPA (alteplase, tenecteplase) dissolves clots in stroke, MI and massive PE. Plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 opposes it.

plasmin_e.name: Plasmin
plasmin_e.notes: Cuts cross-linked fibrin into fibrin degradation products, including D-dimer.

groups.name: Intrinsic pathway
groups.notes: Started by contact with negatively charged surfaces (factor XII). Measured by the PTT; heparin is monitored with it. Hemophilia A (VIII) and B (IX).

groups.name: Extrinsic pathway
groups.notes: Tissue factor with factor VII: the main start of coagulation in the body. Measured by the PT/INR; warfarin is monitored with it (VII has the shortest half-life).

groups.name: Common pathway
groups.notes: Factors X, V, II (prothrombin), I (fibrinogen) and XIII. X → Xa (with Va: prothrombinase) turns prothrombin into thrombin, which turns fibrinogen into fibrin; XIIIa cross-links it. Direct Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban) and direct thrombin inhibitors (dabigatran, argatroban, bivalirudin) act here.

groups.name: Fibrinolysis
groups.notes: tPA turns plasminogen into plasmin, which breaks cross-linked fibrin into fibrin degradation products (D-dimer).
